fatal_errors: The hypothesis assigns the critical increase in ordering to B2 domains, whereas the target mechanism centers on enhanced L12 ordering in the FCC domains approaching Ni3Al stoichiometry.
It replaces the critical jagged B2/FCC phase-boundary morphology and stress concentration at jagged tips with an unsupported coherent-to-incoherent interface transition.
The proposed 400-600°C intermediate range misses the approximately 550-750°C brittle window and does not identify the 600°C ductility minimum or 750°C recovery.
The cited dislocation evidence concerns SRO effects in BCC MoNbTaW and does not establish cross-slip locking in ordered L12 domains of AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
explanation: The response correctly identifies a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition controlled by chemical order and phase boundaries rather than grain-boundary impurity segregation or grain coarsening. It also plausibly connects ordering to restricted dislocation motion and proposes TEM/APT measurements that could partly distinguish intragranular or phase-boundary processes from grain-boundary segregation. However, the central structural mediator is reconstructed incorrectly: the target is enhanced L12 order in the FCC phase together with jagged B2/FCC boundaries, elevated APB energy and modulus, planar slip, pile-ups, and stress concentration at jagged boundary tips. The response instead emphasizes B2 SRO, cross-slip locking, coarsening, and loss of interface coherence. Its recovery mechanism omits reduced L12 ordering and ductile transition zones along phase boundaries. The regime boundary is qualitative and numerically inconsistent with the target. The evidence establishes the starting FCC/B2 alloy and generic SRO-dependent dislocation behavior, but it does not directly support the claimed ordered-domain mechanism in this alloy. A stronger falsification test would map impurity segregation at grain boundaries while directly locating dislocation pile-ups and crack initiation at jagged phase-boundary tips across samples aged below 550°C, near 600°C, at 750°C, and above 750°C.
